dryRun.title: function f() { try { return "try" } finally { log("finally") } }
dryRun.note: An error thrown in try jumps to catch; finally runs no matter what, even after return. A return inside finally overrides everything else, including a thrown error. Errors not caught travel up the call stack.

think.q:
function f() { try { return 1 } finally { console.log('cleanup') } }
console.log(f())
why: finally runs before the function actually returns, so cleanup prints first.
think.exec:
function f() { try { return 1 } finally { console.log('cleanup') } }
console.log(f())

think.q:
function f() { try { throw new Error('x') } finally { return 'swallowed' } }
console.log(f())
why: A return in finally replaces the pending error. The error is lost, which is why return in finally is a bug magnet.
think.exec:
function f() { try { throw new Error('x') } finally { return 'swallowed' } }
console.log(f())

think.q:
function a() { b() }
function b() { throw new Error('deep') }
try { a() } catch (e) { console.log(e.message) }
why: The error travels up from b through a to the nearest catch.

think.q:
try {
  setTimeout(() => { try { throw new Error('later') } catch { console.log('inner') } })
} catch { console.log('outer') }
console.log('after')
why: The outer try/catch only covers code running now: scheduling the timer. The callback throws later, on an empty stack, where only its own try/catch can catch it.

think.q: What is wrong with try { const data = JSON.parse(s); render(data) } catch { showError("bad JSON") }?
opts: It also catches bugs inside render and wrongly reports them as bad JSON
why: Keep try blocks small: only around the line that can fail in the way you are handling.

try.task: Write safeParse(text, fallback): return { ok: true, value } for valid JSON, or { ok: false, error, value: fallback } where error is the SyntaxError message. Do not swallow other kinds of errors.
try.hint: Catch, check e instanceof SyntaxError, and rethrow anything else.

checks.verify: const r = safeParse('{"a":1}'); assert(r && r.ok === true && r.value.a === 1, "valid")

checks.t: invalid JSON gives the fallback and a message
checks.verify: const r = safeParse("{", 42); assert(r && r.ok === false && r.value === 42 && typeof r.error === "string" && r.error.length > 0, "invalid")
let thrown = false; try { safeParse({ toString() { throw new RangeError("boom") } }) } catch (e) { thrown = e instanceof RangeError }; assert(thrown, "should rethrow")

takeaway.key: try/catch catches synchronous throws in its block; finally always runs; never return from finally. Keep try blocks small and rethrow what you do not handle.
mistakes: Huge try blocks that hide unrelated bugs.
Expecting try/catch to catch errors thrown later in callbacks.

dryRun.title: Which error is it?
rows: wrong kind of value for the operation
dryRun.note: All built-in errors inherit from Error and carry name, message and stack. Check the type with instanceof (or name), never by matching message text.

think.q:
const tries = [() => x.y, () => null.y, () => (1).toFixed(200), () => JSON.parse('{')]
console.log(tries.map((f) => { try { f() } catch (e) { return e.name } }).join(' '))
why: Unknown name → ReferenceError, property of null → TypeError, toFixed(200) → RangeError, bad JSON → SyntaxError.
think.exec:
const tries = [() => x.y, () => null.y, () => (1).toFixed(200), () => JSON.parse('{')]
console.log(tries.map((f) => { try { f() } catch (e) { return e.name } }).join(' '))

think.q:
const e = new TypeError('bad')
console.log(e instanceof Error, e.name, String(e))
why: TypeError extends Error. String(e) is "name: message".
think.exec:
const e = new TypeError('bad')
console.log(e instanceof Error, e.name, String(e))

think.q: try { throw 'just a string' } catch (e) { console.log(typeof e, e.stack) }
why: You can throw anything, but a string has no stack trace or name. Always throw Error objects.
think.exec: try { throw 'just a string' } catch (e) { console.log(typeof e, e.stack) }

think.q:
const e = new Error('top', { cause: new Error('db down') })
console.log(e.cause.message)
why: The cause option keeps the original error when you wrap it with a clearer message.
think.exec:
const e = new Error('top', { cause: new Error('db down') })
console.log(e.cause.message)

think.q: Your function gets a negative quantity. Which error fits best?
why: The type is right (a number) but the value is outside the allowed range.

try.task: Write classify(fn): run fn and return "ok", or "bad-input" for TypeError/RangeError, "bad-syntax" for SyntaxError, and "bug" for anything else (including non-Error throws).
try.hint: Use instanceof checks in order inside catch.

checks.t: type and range errors are bad input, syntax is bad syntax

takeaway.key: Built-in errors: ReferenceError, TypeError, RangeError, SyntaxError, URIError, AggregateError. Branch on type, throw Error objects, wrap with { cause }.
mistakes: Matching e.message text to decide what happened.

dryRun.title: class NotFoundError extends Error
rows: so logs and String(e) show the real type
dryRun.note: Custom error classes give each failure a type you can check and fields you can read (status, code, field name). Set name so stack traces say what happened.

think.q:
class AppError extends Error {}
const e = new AppError('x')
console.log(e.name, e instanceof AppError, e instanceof Error)
why: Without setting this.name, the name is inherited from Error.prototype: "Error".

think.q:
class HttpError extends Error { constructor(status, msg) { super(msg); this.name = 'HttpError'; this.status = status } }
const e = new HttpError(404, 'nope')
console.log(String(e), e.status)
why: String(e) uses name and message. The status is a real field.

think.q:
class ValidationError extends Error { constructor(field) { super(field + ' is invalid'); this.name = this.constructor.name; this.field = field } }
class EmailError extends ValidationError {}
console.log(new EmailError('email').name)
why: this.constructor.name gives the actual subclass name, so subclasses do not need their own constructor.

think.q: try { throw new Error('boom', { cause: 'disk' }) } catch (e) { console.log(e.message, e.cause) }
why: cause can be any value, usually the original error.
think.exec: try { throw new Error('boom', { cause: 'disk' }) } catch (e) { console.log(e.message, e.cause) }

think.q: Why are typed errors better than returning null on failure?
opts: null is not allowed in JavaScript
The caller learns WHY it failed and cannot accidentally ignore it
why: null forces callers to guess what went wrong.

try.task: Create class HttpError extends Error with status, and class NotFoundError extends HttpError (status 404, name "NotFoundError"). Then write toResponse(err) returning { status, message }: the error's status for HttpErrors, else 500 with message "Internal error".
examples: toResponse(new NotFoundError("no user"))  // { status: 404, message: "no user" }
try.hint: Set this.name = this.constructor.name in HttpError; NotFoundError calls super(404, message).

checks.verify: const e = new NotFoundError("no user"); assert(e.status === 404 && e.name === "NotFoundError" && e instanceof HttpError && e instanceof Error, "class")
const r = toResponse(new NotFoundError("no user")); assert(r && r.status === 404 && r.message === "no user", "404")
const r = toResponse(new Error("secret")); assert(r && r.status === 500 && r.message === "Internal error", "500")

takeaway.key: Extend Error, call super(message, options), set name, add structured fields. Branch with instanceof.
mistakes: Forgetting this.name, so logs say just "Error".
Leaking internal messages of unexpected errors to users.

dryRun.title: A bug hunt, in order
rows: can I make it fail on demand?
what are the values right there?
dryRun.note: The stack trace is the most useful text in debugging: read it top-down to find your own code. Use breakpoints (or the debugger statement) instead of guessing, and console.table, console.time, console.trace for quick looks.

think.q: console.log([1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2), String([1, 2, 3]))
why: console.log prints arrays in an inspect format, while String() joins with commas. When logging, prefer the object itself over string concatenation.

think.q:
const obj = { n: 1 }
const log = []
log.push(JSON.stringify(obj))
obj.n = 2
console.log(log[0])
why: Logging a copy (JSON.stringify) captures the value at that moment. Browsers show live objects in the console, which can mislead you.
think.exec:
const obj = { n: 1 }
const log = []
log.push(JSON.stringify(obj))
obj.n = 2
console.log(log[0])

think.q:
function f() { return new Error('where').stack.split('\n')[1].includes('at f') }
console.log(f())
why: A stack trace lists the call path, innermost first; line 2 is the function where the Error was created.
think.exec:
function f() { return new Error('where').stack.split('\n')[1].includes('at f') }
console.log(f())

think.q:
const t0 = performance.now()
for (let i = 0; i < 1e5; i++) {}
console.log(typeof (performance.now() - t0))
why: performance.now() gives a high-resolution millisecond number for timing (console.time does the same with a label).

think.q: A user reports "the total is wrong sometimes". What is your first step?
opts: Find an input that reproduces it every time
why: Without a reliable reproduction you cannot tell if a fix worked.

try.task: Write findFirstBad(items, isGood): items go from all good to all bad at some point. Return the index of the first bad item using binary search (like git bisect), or -1 if all are good. isGood must be called at most ~log2(n)+2 times.
try.hint: lo = 0, hi = n. While lo < hi: mid; if good, lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid. Answer lo (or -1 if lo === n).

checks.verify: const big = Array.from({ length: 1024 }, (_, i) => i < 700); let calls = 0; const r = findFirstBad(big, (x) => (calls++, x)); assert(r === 700 && calls <= 12, "too many calls: " + calls)

takeaway.key: Reproduce, read the stack, inspect with breakpoints, narrow down by halving, then lock the fix with a test.
mistakes: Changing code before you can reproduce the bug.
Trusting a live object in the console that changed after logging.
